title: Summary: Choosing and Justifying with Fractions

blocks.text: Understand the Problem Before Choosing a Method

In this review, you must decide how the given information is related. Two quantities may be added or compared, or different expressions may describe the same number. Look at the question and the unit first: having several denominators does not always mean you must find a common one. A common denominator is useful for counting parts of the same size; common factors are useful for simplifying a single fraction.

Work in three stages. First, interpret what you know and what you need to find. Next, choose a representation and preserve the value through each transformation. Finally, check the sign, magnitude, and unit. You can express the result in different equivalent forms when simplification is not required. If simplest form is requested, the denominator must be positive and no common divisor greater than one must remain.

A short argument should connect the given information to the conclusion. "Because I did the calculation" does not explain why that calculation answers the problem. In the following questions you can select a justification or method: use that opportunity to identify mistakes even when a numerical answer seems plausible. No calculator is needed; the quantities were chosen so that the relationships and checks remain clear.

blocks.prompt: There are 5/3 m of ribbon. A label uses 7/12 m and another uses 3/4 m. How many meters remain?

feedback.correct: 5/3 = 20/12, and the two labels use 7/12 + 9/12 = 16/12. There are 4/12 = 1/3 m left. Both amounts used must be subtracted from the total.
feedback.incorrect: Do not subtract only the second label or add the denominators. The ribbon used is 4/3 m, less than 5/3 m, so a positive amount remains.

blocks.text: Numbers in a list can use different partitions. To order them, first identify negative numbers, zero, and positive numbers. Then choose benchmarks or common denominators within each group. If you find two equivalent representations, they are not strictly ordered; here different values have been chosen so that each card has its own place.

blocks.prompt: Arrange from least to greatest. Do not compare only the numbers written above the fraction bars.

feedback.correct: −7/8 < −2/3 < 1/6 < 5/12 < 4/3. Among the negatives, −21/24 is less than −16/24; among the positives, 2/12 < 5/12, and 4/3 exceeds one.
feedback.incorrect: A negative number farther from zero is smaller. 4/3 cannot go among the positive proper fractions because it exceeds one unit.

blocks.prompt: A record starts at −5/12 units and increases by 7/18 units. Enter the new value and choose why its sign makes sense.

options.label: It is negative: 5/12 is greater than 7/18, so the increase does not fully offset it.
options.reviewFeedback: Check the comparison of magnitudes supporting your sign. Express the starting state and the increase as equal-sized parts without confusing their roles.

options.label: It is positive because adding always increases the value past zero.
options.reviewFeedback: Your statement assumes every increase crosses the origin. Check how far the starting state is from zero and how large the change is.

options.label: It is zero because the numerators and denominators cancel one another.
options.reviewFeedback: Your argument cancels digits without examining their values. Express the quantities using equal-sized parts and consider what is being added.

feedback.correct: −5/12 + 7/18 = −15/36 + 14/36 = −1/36. The increase brings the value closer to zero, but it is still one thirty-sixth short.
feedback.incorrect: Increasing a negative number does not guarantee a positive result. Numerator and denominator digits do not cancel either: here only fourteen of the fifteen negative thirty-sixths are offset.

blocks.text: An equivalence describes a value, whereas a fraction of a quantity depends on the unit taken as the whole. Keep this distinction in mind when reading labels on containers, dividing things up, or measuring. An equality can be correct even when its notation is inconvenient; an interpretation can be wrong even if the isolated calculation is correct.

blocks.prompt: Simplify 84/126 with a positive denominator and state the greatest common divisor used. All three fields refer to the same simplification.

feedback.correct: 84 = 42 × 2 and 126 = 42 × 3. The GCD is 42, and the simplest form is 2/3; two and three share no divisor greater than one.
feedback.incorrect: Dividing by six gives 14/21, which is equivalent but not in simplest form. A factor can be canceled only if it divides the entire numerator and the entire denominator.

blocks.prompt: Seven meters of rope are shared equally among six teams. What length does each team receive? No particular simplified form is required.

feedback.correct: Each team receives 7/6 m. The six teams first receive one meter each and share the remaining meter in sixths.
feedback.incorrect: 6/7 reverses the division. 1/6 distributes only the remaining meter and forgets the meter already given to each team. The correct share exceeds one meter.

blocks.prompt: Select all statements that preserve the meaning of a fraction.

options.label: 12/18 and 2/3 represent the same number.
options.reviewFeedback: For the chosen equality, check that the transformation of the numerator and denominator preserves the same multiplicative relationship.

options.label: To add 1/4 and 1/6, I can use twelfths.
options.reviewFeedback: For the selected method, check whether the proposed partition can express each addend without changing its value.

options.label: In (4 + 8)/4 I can cancel the first four and leave 1 + 8.
options.reviewFeedback: For the selected transformation, identify the extent of the division over the sum and distinguish addends from cancelable factors.

options.label: Half of 8 m and half of 10 m have equal lengths.
options.reviewFeedback: For the selected statement, review the whole that each half refers to. Compare physical quantities using the same unit of length.

options.label: −6/9 and 6/−9 represent the same negative number.
options.reviewFeedback: For the chosen equality, interpret the sign of each quotient and check that their magnitudes are equivalent.

feedback.correct: 12/18 simplifies to 2/3; twelfths allow fourths and sixths to be combined; a single negative sign may be placed in either the numerator or the denominator.
feedback.incorrect: In (4 + 8)/4, the entire sum is divided: 1 + 2 = 3, not 9. Half of different lengths gives 4 m and 5 m: the same fraction does not imply the same physical quantity.

blocks.text: If an answer fails your check, identify what changed: the value, sign, unit, or required form. Correcting that point is more useful than mechanically repeating the same calculation.

blocks.prompt: A record begins at −3/4. It first decreases by 1/6, then increases by 5/8. Enter the final value and decide whether it reached zero.

options.label: Yes, because the last change is positive.
options.reviewFeedback: Your decision only considers the last change. Check the position just before it and whether that change was enough to reach the origin.

options.label: No: the result is still negative; the increase does not offset the initial position and the decrease.
options.reviewFeedback: Check your conclusion by keeping the starting state and both changes. Verify the sign of the result using equal-sized parts.

options.label: Yes: any increase cancels out previous decreases.
options.reviewFeedback: Your argument assumes any increase completely cancels the decreases. Examine the sizes of the changes and the starting state.

feedback.correct: In twenty-fourths: −18/24−4/24+15/24 = −7/24. The last increase reduces the distance to zero, but does not reach it.
feedback.incorrect: The direction of the last change does not determine the final sign. Keep all the changes and their signs.

blocks.prompt: For 18/30+7/10, someone cancels the three in thirty and concludes 18/10+7/10. Which correction preserves both addends?

options.label: 18/30 = 3/5 = 6/10; thus the sum is 13/10.
options.reviewFeedback: Check that the simplification preserves the first addend and that the new partition lets you combine it with the second without changing either value.

options.label: You must first add 18+7 and 30+10.
options.reviewFeedback: Your correction adds denominators as well as numerators. Check the size of the parts in each addend before combining quantities.

options.label: The cancellation is correct because thirty has a factor of three.
options.reviewFeedback: Having a factor in the denominator is not enough to cancel it. Check how the numerator must also be transformed to preserve the quotient.

feedback.incorrect: Canceling a factor from the denominator requires canceling it from the numerator too. Adding numerators and denominators does not combine equal-sized parts.

blocks.prompt: The marks on the number line are one sixth apart. Read the point and state how far it must move to the right to reach zero.

feedback.correct: The position is −5/6; moving right by 5/6 brings it to zero. Position and displacement have different signs.
feedback.incorrect: Five intervals to the left give a negative position. The movement to the right has a positive value.

blocks.prompt: A mark lies exactly halfway between 7/6 and 3/2. What is its position?

feedback.incorrect: Adding the endpoints without taking half gives a different point. Comparing with both endpoints checks the construction.
